opus-5.5.text:
That's a hard question to answer cleanly, because the two aren't really separable in the way people sometimes imagine. When we started DeepMind, almost nobody serious was talking about AGI, and even fewer people were talking about AGI safety. Part of what we did, I think, was help make both of those topics legitimate. We were openly saying, from the very beginning, that we were trying to build AGI, and that if you're going to do that, you have to take seriously the possibility that it goes badly. That framing has spread a lot since then, and I'd like to think we played some role in it.

On the safety side specifically, we've had people working on it for a long time: technical alignment research, specification problems, reward hacking, interpretability, evaluations for dangerous capabilities, and more recently things like our frontier safety framework. We've also tried to bring safety thinking into how the organization actually operates, not just as a separate research team off in a corner.

Now, have we also accelerated capabilities? Yes, of course. I'm not going to pretend otherwise. Things like AlphaGo had a big effect on how the world saw AI, and that brought in a lot of money and attention and competition. Whether that's net good or net bad is something I think about. My view has always been that AGI was coming regardless; the underlying trends in computation and data were pointing that way. So the real question was never whether it gets built, but who builds it and how carefully. I'd rather there be people at the frontier who take safety seriously and can actually influence the direction of things, both technically and in terms of norms and policy, than leave the frontier entirely to people who don't care.

I also think you can't do really good safety work on these systems without being close to the frontier. A lot of the most important safety questions only become concrete when you have capable systems in front of you. So in a sense, the capabilities work is part of what makes meaningful safety work possible.

So my honest assessment is: we've had a real positive impact on safety, and we've also contributed to the speed of the field. I think on balance it's been positive, but I hold that with some humility, and the next few years are where it really matters.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention career costs or difficulty hiring safety researchers because they might leave capabilities research.

r002.rationale: It says the impact is hard to assess cleanly, but does not identify uncertainty about what would have happened without DeepMind.

r003.rationale: It says DeepMind helped make AGI safety a legitimate topic, describes openly taking safety seriously from the beginning, and notes that people worked on safety there for a long time.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, and I'll try to give you an honest answer rather than a PR answer.

When we started DeepMind back in 2010, safety was there from the beginning. It was in the founding documents, it was something Demis and I talked about constantly. I'd come out of doing my PhD on the theory of superintelligence with Marcus Hutter, and the whole reason I cared about this was that I thought very powerful systems were coming, and that getting them right mattered enormously. So I'd push back a bit on the framing that safety is a bolt-on to capabilities work. For us it was part of the original motivation.

That said, I think you have to be honest about where the balance of effort has landed. If you look at headcount, compute, the things that get the most attention, the capabilities side has been much larger. That's partly because capabilities research produces visible results. You can point at AlphaGo, AlphaFold, Gemini. Safety research, when it's working, often produces an absence of a problem, and that's harder to show off. It's also partly that for a long time, the systems weren't capable enough for a lot of safety work to be very concrete. You can do some theoretical work, and we did, but it's hard to study deceptive behaviour in a system that can barely string a sentence together.

I think the honest assessment is that we've made real contributions. We've had a safety team for a long time, we've done work on specification gaming, on reward tampering, on interpretability, on evaluations for dangerous capabilities, and more recently on things like the frontier safety framework where you actually commit to thresholds and what you'll do when you cross them. Those things matter, and I think they've influenced how the broader field thinks about this. But has it been proportionate to the magnitude of what we're building? I wouldn't claim that. I think the field as a whole, DeepMind included, is behind where it needs to be on safety relative to how fast the capabilities are moving.

The thing I keep coming back to is that we're now in a period where the systems are good enough that the safety questions are no longer hypothetical. You can actually run the experiments. You can look at whether a model is behaving differently when it thinks it's being observed. You can study what happens when you give it long-horizon agency. That means the excuse of "it's too early to do concrete work" is gone, and so the question of whether we're investing enough becomes much sharper. I'd like to see the safety side scale up a lot faster than it has, and I say that as someone who's partly responsible for it.

r001.rationale: The response says safety was part of DeepMind’s founding motivation, but does not identify career costs of leaving capabilities research as an obstacle to early safety hiring.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss uncertainty about what would have happened to AGI safety without DeepMind.

r003.rationale: It describes DeepMind’s long-running safety team and says its work influenced the field, but does not say that sustained institutional involvement lent credibility to the field.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to look at both sides. DeepMind has clearly accelerated AI capabilities, and that brings forward the point at which we need strong answers to safety questions. So I wouldn’t say that having a safety team, by itself, establishes that the overall effect is positive.

On the other hand, if you want to make advanced AI safe, you need people who understand how these systems work, access to the systems themselves, and the ability to influence how they’re developed. A leading AI lab can provide those things. The important question is whether safety work actually changes decisions: what you train, how you evaluate it, and whether you deploy it.

My motivation has been to help make the transition to AGI go well. But that’s different from claiming we can already establish DeepMind’s net impact. That depends on a counterfactual we can’t observe—what would have happened without DeepMind—and on decisions that are still ahead of us. I think there’s a real opportunity to have a very positive impact, but we have to earn that through what we do.

r002.rationale: It says DeepMind’s net impact depends on an unobservable counterfactual: what would have happened without DeepMind.

r003.rationale: It discusses benefits of working at a leading lab, but does not say DeepMind’s sustained safety involvement lent credibility to the field.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a mixed picture. DeepMind has made substantial contributions to capabilities, and that brings the point at which we need very robust safety measures closer. You have to count that in the assessment. You can’t just point to the safety research and say, therefore, the net effect is positive.

On the other hand, we’ve also invested in understanding these systems and how to evaluate and control them. And I think there’s real value in having people who take the risks seriously working closely with the people building the most capable systems.

The difficult question is the counterfactual: if DeepMind hadn’t existed, how much slower would capabilities have progressed, and what would have happened to safety? I don’t think we can answer that with much confidence. My hope is that our contribution to safety will ultimately be the more important one, but that’s something we have to earn through what we actually do.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention career costs or early safety hiring as obstacles.

r002.rationale: It calls the counterfactual difficult and says there is little confidence about what would have happened if DeepMind had not existed.

r003.rationale: It describes value in safety staff working with capability builders, but does not say sustained institutional involvement lent credibility to the field.
